title: Split the money, keep the average
hook: Does spreading money across bets cost you returns? Or just risk?

knows: expected value: the average result over many tries
that two coin flips can land four ways
doesNotKnow: that splitting across independent bets cuts the chance of the worst outcomes without changing the average
that this depends on the bets being independent

misconception: Splitting your money must lower what you expect to make.
objective: The learner can explain that splitting money across independent bets leaves the average unchanged while making extreme outcomes rarer, because the bets partly cancel, and that this needs independence.

claims.text: Half the time one bet rises and one falls, for +5%.
The average stays +5% however many bets the money is split across.
claims.source: Each bet's expected return is 0.5 × 20 + 0.5 × (−10) = 5; an equal split's expected return is the average of the bets' expected returns, 5, for every n. Demo.tsx average(n) enumerates the binomial outcomes. | v7 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-296, phone fit): reveal sentence shortened to 'The average stayed +5%.' ('as with one bet' cut). Unverified because the text changed. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node port: average(n) = 5.000000 for n = 1..6 in both modes (linearity: 0.5×20 + 0.5×(−10) = 5 per bet). Reveal 'The average stayed +5%' and the Average readout ret(average(n, mode)).

Own node port: the −10% bar's label (outcomes(n)[0].p) is 50%, 25%, 12.5%, 6.3%, 3.1%, 1.6% for n = 1..6 independent, i.e. 0.5^n rendered by pct(). Worst-result readouts are gone in v7; the bar label is the only place the chance appears, and it matches.

claims.text: When the bets move together, any split loses 50% of the time, like one bet; splitting only cancels risk when the bets do not fall together (reveal names the last together split the learner tried).
claims.source: Perfectly correlated bets all return the same, so an equal split returns +20% or −10% with chance 1/2 each, whatever n (Demo.tsx outcomes(n, 'together')). This is the extreme case (correlation 1); for partly correlated bets the cancelling is partial. recall.question: You split money equally between two independent bets with the same average return. Compared with putting it all in one, what changes?
options: The average stays the same; the worst outcome gets rarer
recall.why: Each bet has the same average, so the split does too. Both have to go badly for the worst case, which is less likely than one going badly.
